newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Mitterrand aide is new French foreign minister.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Mitterrand aide is new French foreign minister.

text.p: Hubert Vedrine, appointed France's foreign minister on Wednesday, has a long experience of the delicate art of "cohabitation", as the French call power-sharing between a president and government of different parties.
He is also one of Paris' leading experts on strategy and international relations and published an authoritative book on late president Francois Mitterrand's foreign policy last year.

Vedrine, 49, who takes a portfolio that will involve travelling abroad with conservative Gaullist President Jacques Chirac, earned his spurs as diplomatic adviser, strategic affairs adviser, spokesman and chief aide to Mitterrand.
"We won't need to break him in, he knows the ministry inside out," a senior foreign ministry said.

He has criticised Chirac's moves to bring France back into NATO's U.S.-led military wing, saying Paris should not make concessions without achieving a real shift of power to the Europeans within the Atlantic Alliance.
But when other Socialists criticised a joint Franco-German defence strategy document leaked in January, Vedrine defended it as largely a recapitulation of Mitterrand's defence agreements with Bonn.

A cool administrator, he was one of a handful of officials to serve in the Elysee palace from the day Mitterrand took office in 1981 until the day he left in 1995, latterly as the powerful general-secretary of the president's office.

He was closely involved in foreign and defence policy when Chirac was prime minister under the first "cohabitation" in 1986-88 and was the president's key link-man with Gaullist prime minister Edouard Balladur during the second "cohabitation" in 1993-95, when Mitterrand was weakened by prostate cancer.

In Mitterrand's office, he worked closely with Elisabeth Guigou, the late president's European affairs expert, who was appointed (justice) minister in Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's new cabinet on Wedneday.
After Mitterrand left office, Vedrine returned to private practice as a lawyer.

The son of Jean Vedrine, a World War Two resistance comrade of Mitterrand, he joined the Council of State, France's highest administrative court, after graduating from the elite Ecole Nationale d'Administration civil service college.
He served briefly at the Foreign Ministry from 1979 to 1981 041806 GMT jun 97
